conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during this stay. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not good. Same as always—nauseous, stomach pain, can’t keep anything down. It feels like my usual flare-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned this feels like your typical gastroparesis episodes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. But this time there’s a burning in my upper belly, more than usual. It’s different. I’m just so tired of this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. That burning could be related to acid reflux. We’ll look into that. Your blood sugar was very high when you came in—691. They gave you insulin in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I didn’t know it was that high. Did that make me sicker?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: High blood sugar can definitely make gastroparesis worse. It slows digestion even more. We’re holding your sliding scale insulin for now and just giving your regular NPH to avoid lows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Can I get something for pain? Dilaudid helps best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re avoiding Dilaudid because of your allergies. But we can give you oxycodone for now, and we’ll manage nausea with lorazepam.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright… I just want to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs came back. Your creatinine is up a bit—from your baseline of 1.6 to 2.0. But it’s coming down now, so your kidneys are likely just stressed from dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that bad? My last admission they said I had kidney issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have stage III chronic kidney disease from diabetes. This was a temporary bump. We’re keeping you on lisinopril, which helps protect your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. And my blood pressure was high earlier—was that from the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely. It’s improved now. We’re continuing your amlodipine and lisinopril. They’re safe with your kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s your stomach today? Any nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. I sipped some broth last night. The burning feeling is less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We think that burning might be from acid reflux—GERD. So we’ve started you on a medication called omeprazole twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Omeprazole? I’ve taken that before. Will it help prevent these flares?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might. If acid is triggering your gastroparesis, controlling it could reduce how often you get sick. Your primary doctor and GI specialist are on board with this plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope so. I don’t want to keep coming back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re setting up a care plan with your PCP, psychiatrist, and social work to help prevent that. Your mental health plays a big role in these flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know… anxiety makes everything worse. But I feel stuck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re not alone. The team met with you yesterday, and they’ll keep supporting you. We’re continuing your risperidone and mirtazapine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine test showed protein, which we expected due to diabetic kidney disease. But no infection—culture was negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no UTI? I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, no infection. The protein is from long-term diabetes effects. That’s why managing your blood sugar is so important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I try… but it’s hard when I’m sick and can’t eat regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. That’s why we’re simplifying your insulin—just your usual 70/30 with meals. No extra sliding scale unless we see a real need.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Blood sugar is stable, and your creatinine dropped to 1.6. We’re going to advance your diet to soft foods today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great. Can I try toast or crackers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, start small. We’ll watch how you tolerate it. Less nausea is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I ate half a banana and some applesauce. No vomiting!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent progress. Your body’s starting to reset. We’ll keep the oxycodone available if you need it, but you’re using it less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final update: you’re much improved. Exam shows no abdominal pain, and you’re tolerating food. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Today? That’s fast. What about my blood sugar at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep monitoring your fingersticks like usual. If levels are too high or low, call your doctor. We’re sending you home with omeprazole twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds stay the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—amlodipine, lisinopril, insulin, lorazepam, mirtazapine, risperidone. All continue as before. Follow up with your PCP and psychiatrist soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll try to stick with the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. You’re stronger than you think. Take care, and call if anything worries you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Still a little tired, but my stomach feels okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. Your labs are improving, and you’re walking and eating—great signs. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re cleared to go home. Remember: omeprazole twice a day, monitor sugars, and call your team if you’re struggling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for listening this time. It means a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. We’re on your side. Take it one day at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my hemoglobin test is still pending. Should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was ordered by your PCP for routine monitoring. No results yet, but nothing urgent. They’ll follow up with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I just get anxious when things are pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. That’s why your psychiatrist is staying involved. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you have your prescriptions, ride home, and follow-up appointments scheduled?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I have everything. I’ll call my doctor this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and we hope not to see you back here soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same here. Thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Rest well and keep in touch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling a bit emotional. This cycle is hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s okay to feel that way. You’re doing your best. The team is here to support you through it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try to stay on track with the new medicine and my routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we can ask. You’ve made real progress. Take it one step at a time.
